A.explanation: Speed is not constant because the vertical component of velocity changes under gravity even though the horizontal component is constant.

B.explanation: Speed does not fall linearly to zero because the horizontal velocity never becomes zero and the resultant $v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$ is not linear in $t$.

C.explanation: Speed falls to a non-zero minimum at the top of the path where only the constant horizontal component remains, then rises symmetrically with a curved $\sqrt{}$ shape.

D.explanation: Speed never reaches zero at the top because the horizontal component $v_x$ is unchanged when air resistance is negligible.

hints: Notice the question asks for speed, the magnitude $v = \sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}$, not vertical velocity, and the path shows a symmetric projectile landing on horizontal ground.
Connect the components to free-fall physics: horizontal $v_x$ stays constant while vertical $v_y$ decreases at rate $g$ to zero at the peak and then grows negative.
Compare the minimum value and shape: at the peak $v = |v_x| > 0$, and the square-root combination makes the speed-time curve curved and symmetric, not straight lines to zero.
walkthrough: Resolve the launch velocity into components: horizontal $v_x$ is constant because there is no horizontal acceleration, and vertical $v_y = u_y - gt$ decreases linearly, passes through zero at maximum height, then becomes increasingly negative.
Write speed as the magnitude of velocity: $v = \sqrt{v_x^2 + v_y^2} = \sqrt{v_x^2 + (u_y-gt)^2}$ from $t=0$ at launch to landing.
At the top of the path $v_y = 0$, so $v = |v_x|$. This is the minimum speed and it is greater than zero, which rules out any graph that touches the $t$-axis.
Before the top $|v_y|$ shrinks so $v$ decreases, and after the top $|v_y|$ grows so $v$ increases. The flight over level ground is symmetric, so the fall and rise in speed are mirror images.
Because of the squares and square root, $v$ against $t$ is curved with a flatter slope near the top, not two straight lines. This is option C.
